identity.title: Stress memory and adaptive intelligence in plants from signaling networks to crop improvement under climate change.

content.abstract: Plants, as sessile organisms, have evolved sophisticated decentralized signaling networks that enable perception, integration, and memory of environmental stresses despite lacking a nervous system. This review examines current understanding of plant intelligence, stress memory, and adaptive plasticity, highlighting how these processes enhance survival and productivity under increasingly variable climates. Key mechanisms include sensory receptors for diverse stimuli, rapid signaling via calcium, reactive oxygen species (ROS), electrical, and hydraulic waves, and extensive hormonal crosstalk Abscisic acid (ABA), Jasmonic acid (JA), Salicylic acid (SA), Ethylene (E). Stress memory operates through epigenetic modifications (DNA methylation, histone changes, chromatin remodeling), transcriptional reprogramming (Type I sustained and Type II hyper-induced patterns), and metabolic adjustments that create primed states for faster responses upon recurrent stress. These processes underpin cross-tolerance, systemic acquired resistance (SAR), induced systemic resistance (ISR), and transgenerational inheritance. In crops, priming, microbiome recruitment, and phenotypic plasticity, such as root foraging, shade avoidance, improve resilience to combined abiotic and biotic stresses. Advances in multi-omics, AI-driven phenomics, and systems biology are accelerating the identification of memory-associated genes and regulatory networks. Translational strategies such as seed priming, CRISPR-based editing, and epigenetic-informed breeding offer promising tools for developing climate-resilient varieties with enhanced yield stability. Integrating stress memory and adaptive intelligence concepts offers a comprehensive framework for sustainable agriculture. Future research should prioritize multi-environment field validation, quantification of fitness trade-offs, and integration of multi-stress networks to translate these mechanisms into robust crop improvement strategies.
